stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
Readers have long treated Agnes Marlowe's 1911 novel The Lexicographer's Daughter as a gentle family comedy. Its scenes of a father and daughter quarreling over word definitions are, in this view, light domestic sketches meant chiefly to amuse.

Text 2
Marlowe's novel is certainly funny. But its quarrels over definitions track a real debate of the period: whether dictionaries should record how people actually speak or dictate how they ought to. Beneath the comedy lies a serious argument about language.
choices: The novel's dinner-table setting is its most carefully described location.
The novel's quarrels over word definitions are presented with humor.
The novel is meant mainly to amuse rather than to make an argument.
The novel takes part in a debate over the proper role of dictionaries.
explanation: Text 1 calls the novel a comedy whose quarrels are meant to amuse, and Text 2 opens by granting that the novel 'is certainly funny.' That concession is the shared ground: both authors see the quarrels as humorous. They split over whether anything serious lies underneath.

A.why: You went to a detail from the novel itself instead of the critics' claims about it. Neither author says anything about how carefully any setting is described.

C.why: This is Text 1's view only. Text 2 rejects it and says the comedy covers a serious argument about language.

D.why: This is Text 2's thesis. Text 1 describes the scenes as light sketches and never connects them to a debate about dictionaries.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
Hester Crane's 1894 poem cycle Loom Songs is usually read as a lament. Its speakers, young women in a cotton mill, describe the shuttle's clatter and the endless hours, and critics have taken the poems as straightforward protests against factory labor.

Text 2
Although Loom Songs plainly records the hardship of mill work, its speakers also take pride in their skill, boasting of cloth woven without a single flaw. Crane portrays the weavers as craftswomen, not merely as victims.
choices: Loom Songs presents its weavers as skilled workers proud of their cloth.
Loom Songs is best understood as a simple protest against factory labor.
Loom Songs builds its strongest effects around the sound of the shuttle.
Loom Songs depicts the difficulties of working in a cotton mill.
explanation: Text 1 describes the poems as a lament about the shuttle's clatter and the endless hours. Text 2's concessive clause, 'Although Loom Songs plainly records the hardship of mill work,' accepts the same point. Both agree that the cycle depicts how hard mill work is.

A.why: This is Text 2's new claim. Text 1 reads the poems only as laments and protests and says nothing about pride in skill.

B.why: This is Text 1's reading, and Text 2 argues against it by saying the weavers are more than victims.

C.why: You picked a vivid image from the poems and judged it yourself. Neither critic says the shuttle's sound is where the cycle's strongest effects lie.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
Desmond Ure's 1932 novel The Bran Cure follows a town swept up by a doctor's miracle diet. Most commentators read it as pure satire, a mockery of the era's food fads with no interest in real nutrition.

Text 2
The Bran Cure does ridicule food fads, and its doctor is a fraud. Yet Ure, who corresponded with vitamin researchers, gives the novel's skeptical nurse accurate explanations of dietary deficiency. The book mocks quackery partly by contrasting it with sound science.
choices: The novel ridicules the food fads that were popular in its era.
The novel shows no real interest in the science of nutrition.
The novel's nurse gives accurate explanations of dietary deficiency.
The novel's townspeople are its most memorably drawn characters.
explanation: Text 1 calls the novel 'a mockery of the era's food fads,' and Text 2 grants that it 'does ridicule food fads.' The two critics disagree only about whether the book also takes real nutrition science seriously.

B.why: This is Text 1's position. Text 2 disputes it directly by pointing to the nurse's accurate scientific explanations.

C.why: Only Text 2 makes this claim. Text 1 never mentions the nurse and says the novel ignores real nutrition.

D.why: You gave your own view of the novel's characters instead of anything the critics argue. Neither text ranks the characters.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
Ruth Ansel's 1928 poem "The Coal Fern" describes a fossil frond found in a lump of coal. It is often read as a meditation on mortality, with the ancient plant serving as a reminder that every living thing passes away.

Text 2
Death is undeniably present in "The Coal Fern." But Ansel had studied fossil plants at university, and her poem dwells on how precisely the frond's veins survive in stone. For her, the fossil is less a symbol of loss than a record of endurance.
choices: The fossil in the poem chiefly symbolizes the passing of all living things.
The poem's precise detail reflects Ansel's university study of fossil plants.
The poem engages with the theme of death in some way.
The frond's delicate veins are the most striking image in the poem.
explanation: Text 1 reads the poem as a meditation on mortality. Text 2 concedes that 'Death is undeniably present' before making its own argument. So both critics agree that death is one of the poem's themes.

A.why: This is Text 1's reading. Text 2 says the fossil is 'less a symbol of loss than a record of endurance.'

B.why: Only Text 2 brings up Ansel's university training. Text 1 gives no view on where the poem's detail comes from.

D.why: You read the poem's imagery on your own terms. Text 2 mentions the veins, but neither critic calls them the most striking image.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
Tomas Varga's 1958 novel Hiring Hall, set among dockworkers who gather each dawn hoping to be chosen for a day's work, is widely praised as a portrait of solidarity among workers standing together against the shipping companies.

Text 2
Varga's dockworkers certainly unite against the companies in the novel's climactic strike. Earlier chapters, however, show them competing fiercely for scarce jobs. The novel is really about the tension between solidarity and a labor market with too few openings.
choices: The workers in the novel join together against the shipping companies.
The workers in the novel remain united with one another throughout.
The workers in the novel compete fiercely for a limited number of jobs.
The dawn gatherings at the docks are the novel's most vivid scenes.
explanation: Text 1 praises the novel as a portrait of workers standing together against the shipping companies. Text 2 agrees that they 'certainly unite against the companies' in the strike. That unity is the point both critics share.

B.why: This goes further than the shared point. Text 2 says the workers compete fiercely in the earlier chapters, so it would reject the idea that they stay united throughout.

C.why: This is Text 2's addition. Text 1 describes only solidarity and never mentions competition among the workers.

D.why: You reacted to the novel's setting instead of the critics' arguments. Neither text judges which scenes are most vivid.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
Clara Dunmore's 1903 novel The Night Assistant, about a young woman who catalogs stars at a hilltop observatory, has long been read as a romance. Her nights at the telescope merely set the scene for her courtship with the director's son.

Text 2
The Night Assistant does contain a courtship. But Dunmore devotes far more pages to her heroine's measurements of variable stars than to romance, and the novel ends with her publishing her findings. It is above all a story of scientific ambition.
choices: The heroine's work at the telescope serves mainly as a backdrop.
The novel closes with the heroine publishing her own findings.
The observatory at night creates a lonely and atmospheric setting.
The novel includes a courtship involving its heroine.
explanation: Text 1 reads the novel as a romance built on the heroine's courtship. Text 2 opens by granting that the novel 'does contain a courtship.' The critics disagree about how important it is, but both say it is there.

A.why: This is Text 1's reading. Text 2 says the scientific work is the core of the novel, not a backdrop.

B.why: Only Text 2 describes the ending. Text 1 says nothing about how the novel closes.

C.why: You pictured the setting yourself. Neither critic describes the observatory as lonely or atmospheric.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
Ines Halloway's 1967 novel Grid takes place in a newly built town of identical streets. Critics have generally read it as an attack on modern urban planning, one in which the planners' uniform layout crushes residents' individuality.

Text 2
Halloway is clearly critical of the town's designers in Grid. Her residents, though, are hardly crushed: they repaint doors, plant gardens in the medians, and rename streets. The novel suggests that people reshape even the most rigid plan to suit their own lives.
choices: The town's uniform layout succeeds in crushing residents' individuality.
The novel expresses a critical view of the people who designed the town.
The identical streets of the town give the novel its haunting mood.
The residents adapt the town's rigid plan to suit their own lives.
explanation: Text 1 calls the novel 'an attack on modern urban planning,' and Text 2 grants that Halloway 'is clearly critical of the town's designers.' The critics part ways only on what happens to the residents.

A.why: This is Text 1's reading. Text 2 says the residents 'are hardly crushed.'

C.why: You gave your own impression of the novel's mood. Neither critic says the streets create a haunting atmosphere.

D.why: This is Text 2's thesis. Text 1 sees the residents as crushed by the plan, not as reshaping it.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
Owen Prys's 1979 poem "Aquifer" describes a farming valley in which the wells slowly run dry. Readers have generally treated it as an elegy for a vanished rural way of life, and nothing more.

Text 2
"Aquifer" is certainly elegiac in tone. Still, Prys, a former well driller, describes with technical care how irrigation pumping lowered the water table year after year. The poem mourns the valley, but it also assigns responsibility for the valley's decline.
choices: The poem blames irrigation pumping for the decline of the valley.
The poem's image of empty wells is its most powerful moment.
The poem has a mournful quality suited to an elegy.
The poem is purely an elegy and does not assign blame.
explanation: Text 1 calls the poem an elegy for a vanished way of life. Text 2 grants that it 'is certainly elegiac in tone' and that it 'mourns the valley.' Both critics hear the poem's mournful, elegiac quality.

A.why: Only Text 2 says the poem assigns responsibility. Text 1 says the poem is an elegy 'and nothing more.'

B.why: You picked the poem's central image on your own. Neither critic says which moment is the most powerful.

D.why: This is Text 1's view. Text 2 disputes it by saying the poem 'also assigns responsibility.'
